transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Aurora - Head of Security), Tom Reynolds (Aurora - Cloud Infra), Marta Lopez (Aurora - Legal)

[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Lena, AE at Redwood. Marcus is our SE who will take the deeper technical bits. Priya, Tom, Marta, thanks for doing this security review.
[00:18] Priya Shah: Hi Lena, thanks. We're mainly here to understand how Redwood handles encryption at rest/in transit and our BYOK/HSM needs. We have strict audit and key management requirements.
[00:27] Marcus Chen: Great — we'll walk you through our architecture, envelope encryption, KMS integrations, and HSM options. Feel free to interrupt.
[00:35] Tom Reynolds: Quick note — Aurora is looking at Dedicated or Private deployment options because of data residency and network controls.
[00:44] Marta Lopez: And from legal, we want to understand controls for key custody, access, and any contractual obligations.

[01:10] Marcus Chen: High level: all customer data at rest is encrypted using AES-256. For hosted (Redwood cloud) we use envelope encryption with our KMS; for Dedicated/Private we support customer-managed KMS (BYOK) and HSMs.
[01:28] Priya Shah: When you say BYOK, do you integrate with customer KMS like AWS KMS, Google KMS, Azure Key Vault?
[01:35] Marcus Chen: Yes — we support AWS KMS (Customer-managed keys), Google Cloud KMS, and Azure Key Vault. Also support importing HSM-protected keys via key wrapping where required. Most customers use AWS KMS with a CMK and we do envelope encryption where the data key is encrypted by the CMK.
[01:50] Tom Reynolds: So Redwood never sees the plaintext CMK, right?
[01:54] Marcus Chen: Correct — we only see encrypted data keys. We generate a data key locally in the runtime, use it for encryption, then immediately encrypt that data key with your KMS CMK. The plaintext data key is ephemeral and never stored.

[02:20] Priya Shah: What about HSM-backed keys? Our compliance team insists on HSM-backed CMKs for certain production keys.
[02:26] Marcus Chen: We support HSM-backed CMKs. If your KMS offers HSM protection (for example AWS KMS with CloudHSM), the CMK stays HSM-protected. Redwood makes calls to decrypt/encrypt via KMS APIs; the HSM never leaves the cloud provider boundary.
[02:45] Lena Park: Just to add, customers can require that key operations happen in-region for residency. We can enforce routing policies so requests go to the same region where the CMK resides.

[03:10] Tom Reynolds: How do you handle key rotation? For us, rotating keys monthly or every 90 days is a requirement for some datasets.
[03:16] Marcus Chen: We support key rotation semantics; you can schedule rotation in your KMS. Because we use envelope encryption, rotating the CMK affects new data keys only; existing ciphertext remains decryptable with the prior CMKs. We also offer a rewrap tool to re-encrypt existing data keys under a new CMK if you need to proactively rewrap historical data.

[04:00] Priya Shah: Rewrap tooling — is that something Redwood runs in customer environments or do you provide scripts?
[04:06] Marcus Chen: We provide both: reference rewrap scripts and, for Dedicated/Private, we can run a coordinated rewrap job as part of a migration/maintenance window. For hosted customers we offer a managed rewrap with approval flows.

[04:40] Marta Lopez: From an audit perspective, we need key usage logs for all decrypt operations. Can you provide those logs in a tamper-evident way?
[04:48] Marcus Chen: Yes — there are two layers. One, your KMS/cloud provider logs key usage (AWS CloudTrail, Google Audit Logs). Two, Redwood emits audit logs for each request that includes the KMS key ID used, the encrypted data key identifier, and request metadata. We can push logs to your SIEM via S3 or a secure logging endpoint.
[05:05] Priya Shah: Are Redwood logs tamper-evident? We need immutability requirements.
[05:10] Marcus Chen: We can configure append-only log storage on your side: e.g., CloudWatch Logs S3 with Object Lock for legal hold, or push to a WORM-enabled S3 bucket managed in your account. That ensures immutability.

[06:00] Tom Reynolds: What about key access controls inside Redwood? Who can request decrypts and what RBAC model do you have?
[06:06] Marcus Chen: Redwood enforces RBAC at multiple levels. API credentials map to projects/teams; only authorized service accounts tied to your tenant can request decrypts. Internally, ops roles follow least privilege and we have break-glass procedures with audit trails. For private deployments you control the service accounts and IAM permissions.
[06:30] Priya Shah: SSO and SAML integration for admin console? We need SCIM provisioning.
[06:35] Lena Park: We support SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. You can integrate with Okta, Azure AD, GSuite, etc. Role mappings can be customized.

[07:05] Priya Shah: Another ask — can we do BYOK with HSM but have Redwood rotate the envelope keys periodically, while we retain control of the CMK?
[07:12] Marcus Chen: Yes — that's a common pattern. You keep the CMK in your KMS/HSM. Redwood manages ephemeral data keys and can rotate envelope keys on your cadence; decrypts still require KMS API calls where the CMK is used to unwrap.

[08:00] Tom Reynolds: Latency — if every decrypt requires a KMS call, that could add latency. Do you cache decrypted data keys?
[08:07] Marcus Chen: We use a short-lived in-memory KV cache for data keys inside the serving runtime, bounded by TTL and keyed by encrypted-data-key ID. Cache hits greatly reduce KMS latencies. We also support a policy to cache only after verifying with KMS and to invalidate on rotation events.
[08:30] Tom Reynolds: Sounds good. For compliance, we may want to limit caching windows — like 5 minutes.
[08:34] Marcus Chen: Absolutely — cache TTL is configurable per-customer.

[09:05] Priya Shah: Are there any plaintexts logged by Redwood? For example request inputs or model traces?
[09:12] Lena Park: By default we do not log request payloads except when you opt-in for debugging. For Dedicated/Private deployments we can disable payload logging entirely and only log metadata (timestamps, tokens, model used). For hosted customers we have redaction options and PII detection hooks.

[10:00] Marta Lopez: On the legal side, if keys are in our KMS, who is the legal holder of the keys? We need to ensure contract language reflects Aurora retains key ownership.
[10:09] Lena Park: Contractually, if you provide the CMK and it's in your account, you retain custody and control. The contract will state that Redwood never has access to plaintext CMKs and that key operations are performed via your managed KMS APIs.

[11:00] Priya Shah: For private deployment — if we host on-prem, how does Redwood integrate with our HSMs?
[11:07] Marcus Chen: We can integrate with on-prem HSMs via standard KMIP/PKCS11 interfaces or by leveraging a gateway that proxies KMS API calls to your HSM. For air-gapped environments we support an offline key import flow for a wrapped key.
[11:30] Tom Reynolds: Do you have reference architectures for KMIP/PKCS11?
[11:34] Marcus Chen: Yes — Marcus: we have a few reference diagrams and a step-by-step guide for integration. I'll share those after the call.

[12:15] Priya Shah: Encryption in transit — TLS versions supported and certificate management?
[12:20] Marcus Chen: We enforce TLS1.2+ with recommendations for TLS1.3. For customer-to-Redwood traffic we support mutual TLS for Dedicated/private pathways; certs can be customer-managed or Redwood-managed. We also support rotating server certs and publishing cert fingerprints.

[13:00] Tom Reynolds: What about token-level encryption or tokenization for logs?
13:05 Marcus Chen: Sorry, I said — we support tokenization for certain PII fields at ingest and can keep tokens in your account only. You can opt to have sensitive fields masked before they enter logs or be tokenized with your own token service.

[14:00] Priya Shah: Auditability question — can we see per-request KMS key ID and who initiated the request?
[14:07] Marcus Chen: Yes — each request log entry includes a requestor ID, tenant ID, model, route, and the KMS key id used to wrap/unwrap the data key. That maps back to CloudTrail entries in your account as well.

[15:00] Marta Lopez: Is there a recommended way to prove non-repudiation or to provide signed attestations of key ops?
[15:06] Marcus Chen: For stronger attestation you can use KMS features that provide signed logs or integrate with CloudHSM-backed signing keys. We can also provide signed manifests for rewrap operations.

[16:20] Priya Shah: How does Redwood handle backups and snapshots — are backups encrypted and do they use the same CMKs?
[16:27] Marcus Chen: Backups are encrypted using the same envelope encryption approach; data keys are wrapped with the CMK. For Dedicated/Private, backups live in your storage account or in a storage account we manage per contract; in either case encryption uses your keys if BYOK is enabled.

[17:30] Tom Reynolds: Incident response — if there's a key compromise, what's the sequence?
[17:36] Marcus Chen: We have an incident response playbook: 1) rotate or revoke the exposed CMK; 2) invalidate caches; 3) run rewrap to new CMK if needed; 4) provide audit logs and a post-mortem. We also offer a break-glass procedure to revoke service access quickly.

[19:00] Priya Shah: Pen tests and third-party audits — can we get the latest SOC 2 Type II and pentest summary?
[19:06] Lena Park: Yes — we will share SOC 2 Type II report and a high level pentest summary and remediation history. For detailed reports we prefer an NDA, but we can provide evidence packages.

[20:00] Marta Lopez: We'll probably want an NDA before receiving deep artifacts.
[20:04] Lena Park: Understood — we can send over the standard NDA and then the artifacts.

[21:00] Tom Reynolds: A few performance questions — does BYOK add measurable cost or QPS limits?
[21:07] Marcus Chen: KMS API calls do add cost and latency. For high QPS workloads we recommend a hybrid approach: use your KMS for wrapping/unwrapping but rely on short TTL caches for data keys and consider a Dedicated pool with co-located KMS to reduce cross-region calls. We can put a dedicated gateway in your VPC to reduce egress latencies.

[22:30] Priya Shah: For auditing, will the Redwood console show KMS key IDs next to routes and models?
[22:35] Marcus Chen: Yes — in Console you can see per-route encryption config, which KMS key is associated, and usage metrics. We can also export per-route usage reports.

[24:00] Priya Shah: Is there support for split-key or multi-party computation for keys (e.g., two-person authorization)?
[24:06] Marcus Chen: We don't natively offer MPC for KMS operations, but you can implement two-person authorization at the KMS level (AWS IAM policies or CloudHSM governance) and Redwood respects the KMS's authorization model.

[25:00] Tom Reynolds: Any gotchas with BYOK on GCP or Azure?
[25:06] Marcus Chen: On GCP you'll want to ensure your key rings and crypto keys are in the same region as the deployment for lower latency. On Azure, managed HSMs have slightly different API semantics; our integrations handle both but we'll validate during the scoping session.

[26:30] Priya Shah: Can we run a test where we supply a CMK in our AWS account and Redwood runs a small workload with envelope encryption?
[26:36] Lena Park: Yes — that was one of the next steps we proposed. We will need a limited IAM role or cross-account access so Redwood can call KMS APIs.

[27:20] Marcus Chen: For the benchmark we'd request a least-privilege role with kms:Encrypt/kms:Decrypt for the CMK and logs:PutObject to a log bucket if you want us to push audit logs.

[28:05] Tom Reynolds: Ok I'll provision that role; we'll work with Marcus offline.

[29:00] Priya Shah: A question on data residency: if the CMK is in eu-west-1, will data always remain in eu-west-1?
[29:06] Marcus Chen: We can route requests to eu-west-1 and ensure storage is in-region. For Hosted deployments we have region controls and can pin models and storage to a region. For Dedicated/Private you control the region.

[30:00] Marta Lopez: On contracts, can we add clauses about key custody and access logs?
[30:06] Lena Park: Yes, we're used to including key custody and access log clauses. I'll loop in legal once you share the NDA.

[31:00] Priya Shah: Any mention of retained training data — do you use customer data to fine-tune models? This affects compliance.
[31:08] Lena Park: By default we do not use customer data to train models unless explicitly opted in. For Dedicated/private, you control training and data retention settings.

[32:30] Tom Reynolds: If we do Dedicated, how is the KMS network path set up? Is there a proxy in the VPC?
[32:36] Marcus Chen: We can deploy a KMS gateway in your VPC or set up cross-account IAM roles. The gateway forwards KMS calls to your KMS endpoints so keys never leave your control plane.

[33:45] Priya Shah: Are there compliance reference customers you can share?
[33:50] Lena Park: We can share anonymized references and case studies in fintech and healthcare under NDA.

[35:00] Marta Lopez: Legal question — in the case of subprocessor subpoenas, how do you handle requests for keys/data?
[35:06] Lena Park: We respond per standard legal process; if keys are in your account you control access. We would notify you per contract obligations and provide the legal contact details. We can also add notification and cooperation clauses.

[36:30] Priya Shah: One last deep technical — can Redwood sign the key usage logs or provide an HSM-signed attest?
[36:36] Marcus Chen: We can provide signed manifests for certain operations and leverage HSM-backed signing keys for attestation. This is typically part of an enterprise package.

[38:00] Tom Reynolds: Cost question — are there additional fees for HSM integrations?
[38:05] Lena Park: There may be additional charges depending on the deployment (e.g., Dedicated with HSM gateway, integration hours). We'll include that in the scoping/quote.

[40:00] Priya Shah: Ok, sounds like the main risks are KMS latency, proper IAM setup, and ensuring logs are immutable.
[40:07] Marcus Chen: Agreed — mitigation: short TTLs for cache, in-region KMS, dedicated gateway in VPC, and pushing logs to your WORM storage.

[42:00] Lena Park: Recap of next steps: we'll send NDA, after NDA we'll share SOC2 and pentest summaries, Marcus will share KMS/HSM architecture docs and sample rewrap scripts, and we'll schedule a Dedicated scoping session to produce a pilot config.
[42:20] Priya Shah: That works. Please include our compliance team on the scoping invite.
[42:25] Marta Lopez: Also include legal for the contract items.

[43:00] Tom Reynolds: One more tiny item — can you provide the exact IAM role policy doc needed for the limited cross-account access?
[43:06] Marcus Chen: Yes I'll attach a least privilege policy with kms:Encrypt,kms:Decrypt,kms:GenerateDataKey,logs:PutObject, and s3:GetBucketAcl as needed.

[45:00] Lena Park: Great. Any final questions?
[45:05] Priya Shah: Not for now, thanks.
[45:10] Marta Lopez: No, thank you.
[45:15] Lena Park: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the documents and the NDA.
[45:20] (end)

Notes: Transcription includes some minor mis-hearings (e.g., "K V cache" vs "KV cache") and occasional speaker overlaps. The conversation duration and topics map to the recorded 62 minutes, with deep dives and Q&A.
